AC RIPPLE - The AC voltage component found on DC voltage levels after the rectification and filtering process in a DC power supply. Since power supply rectifiers and filters are not perfect some portion of the original AC signal remains on the DC voltage level after it has been rectified and filtered. Ideally, the AC ripple voltage should be as small as possible.

INTERNAL SHORT

An internal short between two pins of an IC will force the logic signals at those pins always to be identical. Whenever two signals that are supposed to be different show the same logic level variations, there is a good possibility that the signals are shorted together.
To illustrate, consider the input waveforms shown in the diagram. Even though these two inputs are different, the waveforms at Gate1 pin 2 and Gate 2 pin 4 are the same.
During the interval t4 to t5 both INVERTERs have a LOW input and both outputs are trying to produce a HIGH output, again their being shorted together makes no difference.
However, during the intervals t2 to t3 and t3 to t4, one INVERTER is trying to produce a HIGH output while the other is trying to produce a LOW output.
In this situation the actual voltage level that appears at the shorted outputs of the INVERTERs will depend on the internal IC circuitry.

For TTL devices it will usually be a voltage in the high end of the logic 0 range (i.e., close to 0.8V), although it may also be in the indeterminate range. For CMOS devices it will often be a voltage in the indeterminate range.
